headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% for the first time in over three years

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The return investors get from lending to the UK government; it rises when investors want more reward for the risk.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November 2026, its first increase since 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1, with eight members backing a quarter-point rise and one wanting a half-point rise.
The Bank said energy-driven inflation linked to the Iran war was the reason. Annual inflation was 3.5% in September, and the Bank now expects it to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
It raised its growth forecast to 1.6% for this year and 1.3% for 2027, though it said growth was likely to slow in coming quarters. Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. Markets put the chance of another rise in December at about one in four, and the next decision is on 17 December. The 10-year gilt yield was about 5.15% after the announcement, and mortgage rates have risen since September.
levels.why: It sets the cost of borrowing for millions of households and for the government, at a time when prices are rising again.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4%, the first rise since 2023
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%, the first increase in more than three years. Eight of the nine members of its Monetary Policy Committee voted for a quarter-point rise, while one wanted a bigger half-point move.
The Bank blamed inflation driven by energy prices, which have jumped because of the war involving Iran. Inflation stood at 3.5% in September and the Bank expects it to come close to 5% by mid-2027.
Its forecasts show the economy growing 1.6% this year and 1.3% in 2027, but more slowly in the months ahead. Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be read as the start of a long run of rises. Traders think a further increase in December is possible but less likely than not. Government borrowing costs stayed high, with the 10-year gilt yield near 5.15%, and mortgage rates have been climbing since September.
levels.why: Higher rates affect mortgages, savings and government borrowing all at once.

levels.headline: Interest rates rise to 4% as the Bank of England fights energy-driven inflation
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first rise since 2023. Eight policymakers backed a quarter-point increase and one argued for half a point.
The Bank says the main cause is higher energy prices linked to the war with Iran, which are pushing up the cost of living. Inflation was 3.5% in September, and the Bank thinks it will approach 5% by the middle of next year if nothing changes.
The Bank also now expects slightly stronger growth, 1.6% this year and 1.3% next, although it warns that the economy is likely to slow. Governor Andrew Bailey stressed that this rise is not necessarily the first of many. The cost of government borrowing is still high, and mortgage rates have gone up since September. The next decision comes on 17 December.
levels.why: Many families will see the effect on their monthly mortgage payments or savings returns.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since 2023. Eight of nine members of the rate-setting committee voted for the rise, and one wanted a larger one.
The Bank said rising energy costs caused by the Iran war are pushing up prices. Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, was 3.5% in September, and the Bank expects it to reach about 5% by mid-2027.
It expects the economy to grow 1.6% this year and 1.3% in 2027, but more slowly soon. Governor Andrew Bailey said the move was not the start of an inevitable series of rises. Markets see about a one in four chance of another rise in December. Mortgage rates have gone up since September, and the cost of government borrowing remains high, with the ten-year yield around 5.15%. The next decision is due on 17 December.
levels.why: Borrowers and savers will feel the change, and it shows how the Iran war is hitting British pockets.

levels.headline: Interest rates go up to 4% to keep prices under control
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%, up from 3.75%. This is the first rise for more than three years. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money, so a higher rate usually makes loans and mortgages more expensive and savings accounts more rewarding.
The Bank did it because prices are rising faster again, mainly because energy has become more expensive after the Iran war. Prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier in September, and the Bank thinks the figure could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
Eight of the nine decision-makers voted for the rise and one wanted more. Governor Andrew Bailey said it did not mean lots more rises are certain. The Bank still expects the economy to grow, by 1.6% this year, but more slowly later. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings, and how fast prices rise.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates to try to slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise since 2023. The rate is what the Bank charges banks to borrow, and it affects what ordinary people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.
The Bank did this because prices are going up faster. Energy is costing more because of the war involving Iran, and that makes many other things dearer too. In September prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. The Bank thinks that could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
Eight of its nine decision-makers voted for the rise. One wanted a bigger one. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said this is not the start of many rises. It expects the economy to grow, but more slowly soon. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: If you have a mortgage or savings, your monthly money may change.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing a bit more expensive
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates to 4%. They were 3.75%. This is the first rise in over three years. An interest rate is the extra money you pay back when you borrow, or the extra you get when you save.
Why now? Prices are rising faster. Fuel and energy cost more because of a war involving Iran. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The Bank thinks they could go up by about 5% by mid-2027. Raising rates is a way to cool things down, because people spend a little less when borrowing costs more.
Eight of nine members voted yes and one wanted a bigger rise. The boss, Andrew Bailey, said it does not mean many more rises are coming. People with mortgages may pay more each month.
levels.why: It could change how much families pay each month and how quickly prices climb.

levels.headline: Interest rates go up: what the Bank of England did and why
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after money in the UK. It has raised its interest rate from 3.75% to 4%. The interest rate is like a price for borrowing money. When it goes up, loans such as mortgages usually cost more.
The Bank did this because prices are rising too fast. This is called inflation. Oil and gas cost more after a war involving Iran, so many things in shops cost more too. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. The Bank thinks it could reach about 5% next year.
Most of the group that makes the decision voted yes. Eight said a small rise, and one wanted a bigger rise. The Bank says it does not plan lots more rises. Some families will pay more on their home loans.
levels.why: It changes how much money families have left each month.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises its rate to help slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England is in charge of how much it costs to borrow money in the UK. This week it made borrowing a little dearer. It raised its interest rate to 4% from 3.75%.
Why? Prices in shops have been going up faster. That is called inflation. Oil and gas have become more costly because of a war in the Middle East, and that makes lots of things cost more. The Bank wants to stop prices rising too quickly. If borrowing costs more, people tend to spend a bit less, and prices rise more slowly.
Eight of the nine people who decide voted for the rise. One wanted it even bigger. The head of the Bank said this does not mean many more rises are coming. People who owe money on a home may have to pay a little more each month.
levels.why: It is one way the country tries to keep prices from rising too fast.

levels.headline: A big bank makes borrowing cost a little more
levels.body:
There is a big bank in the UK called the Bank of England. It does not look after your pocket money. It looks after the money for the whole country. This week it changed a number called the interest rate. The number went up from 3.75 to 4.
Think of it like this. If you borrow a toy from a friend, you might give back a little extra as a thank you. Interest is the extra that grown-ups pay when they borrow money. Now the extra is a little bigger.
Why did the bank do it? Things in shops are costing more, like petrol and gas for heating. The bank hopes that dearer borrowing will help stop prices going up so fast. Eight people agreed and one wanted an even bigger change. Some families might have a little less spare money.
levels.why: It helps keep the cost of everyday things steady for families.

levels.headline: Wall Street: S&P 500 closes up 0.31% at 7,376.86 after Thursday's tech rout
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up 0.31% at 7,376.86 on Friday 6 November, the last completed session, recovering a small part of Thursday's heavy fall. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.09% to 24,579.42. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to 51,285.73.
On Thursday the S&P 500 had dropped 4.36% to 7,353.73, and the Nasdaq had lost 5.52% to 24,315.00, putting it in correction territory, more than 10% below a record set last month. Nvidia fell more than 9% and the so-called Magnificent Seven lost over $1 trillion in value. Investors feared that a Democratic win in Congress could slow the AI data-centre buildout.
All three major averages still ended the week lower. The Friday figures come from a live market report, so exact closing numbers may differ slightly in final tallies.
levels.why: US share prices affect pensions and savings around the world, including in the UK.

levels.headline: US stocks edge up on Friday after Thursday's sharp tech sell-off
levels.body:
The S&P 500 finished Friday 6 November up 0.31% at 7,376.86, the latest completed session. The Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42, while the Dow slipped 0.46%, or 237.33 points, to 51,285.73.
The small rebound followed a brutal Thursday, when the S&P 500 fell 4.36% and the Nasdaq dropped 5.52%, its worst day since April 2025. That pushed the Nasdaq into a correction, meaning a fall of more than 10% from its October record. Chipmakers were hit hardest, with Nvidia down more than 9%.
Investors worried that Democratic control of Congress after the midterms could curb the AI data-centre boom. Despite Friday's gains, all three main indexes lost ground over the week. Some analysts expect more turbulence ahead. The figures come from a live market report and may be revised slightly.
levels.why: A sharp fall in US tech shares can ripple through global markets and pension funds.

levels.headline: S&P 500 ends Friday higher but the week was still a losing one
levels.body:
The S&P 500 rose 0.31% on Friday 6 November to close at 7,376.86. The Nasdaq gained 1.09% to 24,579.42, but the Dow Jones fell 0.46%, down 237.33 points, to 51,285.73. Friday was the last completed trading session.
The gains were small compared with Thursday's falls. On Thursday the S&P 500 lost 4.36%, and the Nasdaq slumped 5.52%, which put it into what traders call a correction, a drop of more than 10% from its peak. Technology and chip companies led the sell-off, and Nvidia lost over 9%.
Many investors fear that the Democrats' win in the midterm elections could slow spending on AI data centres. All three main US indexes ended the week lower. These numbers come from a live report, so final figures may differ slightly.
levels.why: Big swings in US shares can affect savings and pensions, even for people who never buy shares.

levels.headline: US shares recover a little after the worst tech day in over a year
levels.body:
The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big US companies, closed up 0.31% on Friday 6 November at 7,376.86. The tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42. The Dow, which tracks 30 large firms, fell 0.46% to 51,285.73.
This came after a very bad Thursday, when the S&P 500 fell 4.36% and the Nasdaq fell 5.52%. The Nasdaq is now in a correction, which means it has fallen more than 10% from its recent high. Computer chip makers such as Nvidia were hit hardest.
Investors are nervous that, after Democrats won Congress, rules could slow down the building of data centres for artificial intelligence. Even with Friday's rise, all three main indexes ended the week down. These figures come from a live report.
levels.why: Many people's pensions are invested in these companies, so big falls matter.

levels.headline: American shares rise a little on Friday after a big fall

US shares went up a little on Friday 6 November. The S&P 500, which follows 500 large companies, rose 0.31% to 7,376.86. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, rose 1.09% to 24,579.42. The Dow, which follows 30 big companies, fell 0.46% to 51,285.73.

levels.why: Falling shares can make people feel poorer and cut back on spending.

levels.headline: US stock prices bounce back slightly after a rough day
levels.body:
On Friday 6 November, the S&P 500 went up by 0.31%. It ended at 7,376.86. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big American companies. Their share prices are added up into one number.

levels.why: Many people save for retirement in shares, so these moves matter.

levels.headline: American shares had a small bounce on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. When many people want to buy shares, prices go up. When they want to sell, prices go down. A number called the S&P 500 follows 500 big American companies. On Friday 6 November it went up 0.31%, finishing at 7,376.86.

levels.why: Share prices show how confident people are about the future of companies and jobs.

levels.headline: Share prices wobble in America
levels.body:
In America, people buy and sell tiny pieces of companies called shares. A big list called the S&P 500 follows 500 of those companies. On Friday it went up a little, by 0.31%. It finished at 7,376.86.
Another list, the Nasdaq, has lots of technology firms. It went up too, by 1.09%. A third list, the Dow, followed 30 big companies. It went down a bit, by 0.46%.

At the end of the week, all three lists were lower than at the start.
levels.why: When share prices fall, many grown-ups worry about their savings.

levels.headline: Share prices bounce a little
levels.body:
Imagine the playground has a trading game. Children swap stickers, and some stickers become more popular than others. Grown-ups play a bigger version with shares, which are tiny pieces of companies. America has a big list called the S&P 500 that follows 500 companies. On Friday its number went up a little, to 7,376.86.
Another list, the Nasdaq, with many computer companies, also went up. A third list, the Dow, went down a bit.
The day before, lots of people sold shares, and prices dropped. It was like everyone suddenly wanting to swap away the same sticker. Companies that make computer chips were hit hardest. On Friday some people bought again, so prices bounced back a little. But over the whole week, they were still lower.
levels.why: It shows how worried or hopeful grown-ups feel about money.

levels.headline: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts, as unemployment slips to 4.1%
levels.body:
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the consensus forecast of about 59,000, the Labor Department's report showed on Friday 6 November. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, slightly below the 4.2% economists had expected. Earlier months were revised up, with August now at 186,000 and September at 60,000.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year, and the participation rate, the share of adults in work or looking for it, rose to 61.9%. The weak spot was long-term unemployment: the average spell without work jumped to 27.1 weeks, up 2.3 weeks from September, and about 2 million people, or 27.6% of all jobless workers, had been out of work for 27 weeks or longer.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose after the data. Analysts said the strength strengthened the case for the Federal Reserve to consider raising interest rates again at its December meeting, with inflation still above the bank's 2% target.
levels.why: Strong jobs data can keep American interest rates higher for longer, which affects borrowing costs and markets around the world.

levels.headline: US adds 165,000 jobs in October, far more than expected, and unemployment falls to 4.1%
levels.body:
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than the 59,000 or so that economists had forecast, according to the official report published on Friday 6 November. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1% from a forecast of 4.2%. Figures for earlier months were revised up, to 186,000 for August and 60,000 for September.
Pay grew 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the past year. The participation rate, which counts people who are working or looking for work, rose to 61.9%. However, long-term unemployment is a worry. The average time people spend jobless rose by 2.3 weeks to 27.1 weeks, and about 2 million people, 27.6% of all those out of work, have been jobless for 27 weeks or more.
Bond yields rose after the report. The strong figures gave more support to the idea that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates in December, as inflation remains above its 2% target.
levels.why: Hiring this strong makes higher US interest rates more likely, and that can push up borrowing costs elsewhere too.

levels.headline: American employers add 165,000 jobs in October, well above forecasts
levels.body:
American employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far above the roughly 59,000 that experts had predicted. The figures were published on Friday 6 November. Wages rose 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. More people were in work or looking for it, with the participation rate rising to 61.9%. One weaker point was long-term unemployment. The average time out of work rose to 27.1 weeks, and about 2 million people, or 27.6% of the unemployed, had been without a job for 27 weeks or more.
The yield on US ten-year government debt rose after the report. Strong hiring makes it more likely that the Federal Reserve will consider another interest rate rise in December, because inflation is still above its 2% goal.
levels.why: What happens to US interest rates affects mortgages, savings and share prices well beyond America.

levels.headline: US jobs report: far more jobs than expected in October
levels.body:
The United States added 165,000 jobs in October. That is far more than the 59,000 or so that experts expected. The government published the figures on Friday 6 November. The unemployment rate, the share of people without a job who want one, fell a little to 4.1%. Experts had expected 4.2%. The totals for August and September were also made higher, to 186,000 and 60,000.
Pay went up by 0.4% over the month and 3.1% over the year. More people were working or looking for work. One weak spot was people out of work for a long time. On average, they had been jobless for 27.1 weeks. About 2 million people had been out of work for 27 weeks or more.
The cost of US government borrowing rose after the report. Strong hiring means the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, may raise interest rates in December, because prices are still rising faster than its 2% target.
levels.why: US interest rates affect borrowing costs around the world, including for people in Britain.

levels.headline: America creates many more jobs than expected
levels.body:
America created 165,000 new jobs in October. Experts had expected only about 59,000, so this was a big surprise. The numbers came out on Friday 6 November. The unemployment rate, which shows how many people want a job but cannot find one, fell a little to 4.1%.
Pay also went up. Average pay rose 0.4% in a month, and 3.1% over a year. A few more people joined the workforce too. But there is a worry. Some people have been out of work for a long time. About 2 million people have been without a job for half a year or more.
After the news, the cost of borrowing for the US government went up. America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, sets interest rates, which is the price of borrowing money. With so many jobs, it might raise rates again in December. It wants prices to rise by only 2% a year, and they are rising faster.
levels.why: What America's central bank does with interest rates can change loan and savings costs far away from the US.

levels.headline: America has many more new jobs than expected

levels.headline: America finds many more jobs than expected

levels.headline: Lots of new jobs in America

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September as fuel costs climb
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. It beat the 3.4% that analysts had expected and was the highest rate since October 2025. The ONS also reported CPIH, which includes housing costs for owner occupiers, at 3.6%.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%. Transport was the largest upward contributor, with inflation in that category jumping to 6.6% from 4.6%, driven mainly by motor fuel. Food inflation held at 1.3%.
The figures were published on 21 October and helped cement expectations that the Bank of England would raise interest rates, which it did on 5 November. The next inflation release is due on 18 November, covering October.
levels.why: Rising prices cut the buying power of wages and drive decisions on interest rates.

levels.headline: Inflation climbs to 3.5% as petrol and transport costs rise
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK, as measured by the Consumer Prices Index, rose to 3.5% in the year to September 2026 from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics said. Economists had forecast 3.4%, and this was the highest figure since October 2025. The broader CPIH measure was 3.6%.
Underlying pressure also edged up. Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, increased from 2.6% to 2.8%. The biggest push came from transport, where inflation reached 6.6%, mostly because of higher fuel prices. Food price inflation stayed at 1.3%.
The release on 21 October strengthened the case for a Bank of England rate rise, which followed on 5 November. The next figures, for October, are due on 18 November.
levels.why: It explains why borrowing costs are going up again.

levels.headline: UK prices rose faster in September, with fuel costs the main driver
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in August. The Office for National Statistics published the figure on 21 October. It was a little higher than the 3.4% that experts had predicted, and the highest since October 2025.
A second measure that counts housing costs for people who own their homes was 3.6%. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco because their prices jump around, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%.
The biggest cause was transport, where prices rose 6.6% over the year, mostly because of dearer petrol and diesel. Food prices rose by a slower 1.3%. The numbers helped persuade the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 November. The next update comes on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher prices make wages and benefits stretch less far.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5%, the highest in almost a year
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August. Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a year. The Office for National Statistics, which collects the figures, published them on 21 October. Experts had expected 3.4%, and this was the highest level since October 2025.
Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco because their prices swing a lot, rose from 2.6% to 2.8%. Transport costs rose most, by 6.6% over the year, largely because fuel got dearer. Food prices went up a more modest 1.3%.
The rise made it more likely that the Bank of England would raise interest rates, and it did so on 5 November. The next figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: It shows how far everyday costs are climbing and why rates have risen.

levels.headline: UK prices rise faster, with petrol and diesel a big reason
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in August. This rate of price rises is called inflation. The Office for National Statistics published the figure on 21 October. Experts had expected 3.4%.
The biggest push came from transport, where prices were up 6.6% over the year, mostly because petrol and diesel cost more. Food prices rose more slowly, by 1.3%. A different measure that leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, because their prices jump around, rose from 2.6% to 2.8%.
The Bank of England watches these figures when it sets interest rates, and it raised them on 5 November. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: It shows how fast the cost of living is rising.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in the UK, mainly because of fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising faster. In September they were 3.5% higher than a year before. In August the figure was 3.1%. This rate of price rises is called inflation. The Office for National Statistics, a government body that counts these things, shared the figure on 21 October.
Most of the rise came from transport. Costs there went up 6.6% over the year, mainly because petrol and diesel got dearer. Food prices rose more slowly, by 1.3%. Another measure, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, also rose, from 2.6% to 2.8%.
This was a little more than experts had expected. It is one reason the Bank of England put interest rates up on 5 November. The next figures come out on 18 November.
levels.why: When prices rise faster than pay, people can buy less with the same money.

levels.headline: UK prices went up faster in September
levels.body:
New figures show that prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier. A month before, the figure was 3.1%. When prices keep going up like this, we call it inflation. It means the same money buys a bit less than before.
The biggest reason was transport. Costs there rose 6.6%, mainly because petrol and diesel cost more. Food rose by much less, just 1.3%. The Office for National Statistics, which is a government group that does the counting, shared the numbers on 21 October.
The rise was a bit bigger than experts guessed. It helped lead the Bank of England to raise interest rates on 5 November. The next numbers are due on 18 November.
levels.why: It affects how much shopping, fuel and bills cost your family.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are going up faster
levels.body:
Every month, people called statisticians check how much things cost. They look at things like food, petrol and bus tickets. They compare the prices with a year ago. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. In August, they were 3.1% higher. Prices going up like this is called inflation.
Most of the extra came from transport, mostly because petrol and diesel got more expensive. Transport costs rose by 6.6%. Food went up by less, 1.3%.
The number was a little higher than experts thought it would be. The Bank of England looks at it when it chooses interest rates. It decided to put rates up on 5 November. The next numbers come out on 18 November.
levels.why: It tells us how fast the cost of living is going up.

levels.headline: Things in shops cost a bit more than last year
levels.body:
Prices change over time. A packet of crisps or a bus ticket may cost more this year than last year. When lots of prices go up together, we call it inflation. Experts count it every month. In September, things cost 3.5% more than a year earlier. That means something that cost one hundred pounds now costs about one hundred and three pounds and fifty pence.
The biggest rise was in travel. Petrol and diesel cost more, so travel costs went up by 6.6%. Food went up less, by 1.3%.
Grown-ups at the Bank of England watch these numbers. When prices climb fast, they make borrowing cost more, to slow things down. They did that on 5 November.
levels.why: It helps explain why your family may feel money does not go as far.

levels.headline: Prices creep up
levels.body:
Think of your pocket money. Last year you could buy a sweet for one pound. This year the same sweet costs a few pence more. When lots of things cost a bit more, grown-ups call it inflation. It means the same money buys a little less.
In the UK, prices in September were 3.5% higher than a year before. That is a bit more than the month before. A lot of the rise came from petrol and diesel, which cost more. Food went up by only a little.
People who count prices told everyone the news on 21 October. The grown-ups who look after the nation's money watched it carefully. They decided to make borrowing cost a bit more to slow prices down.
levels.why: It shows why your family's money may not stretch as far.

headline: Healey's Budget cuts energy bills, raises a bank surcharge and lifts the minimum wage

terms.meaning: The gap between the government's forecast borrowing and the limit it has set itself.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the public finances.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget cuts energy bills, raises a bank surcharge and lifts the minimum wage
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October 2026. A one-off payment of £100 will go to 20 million households to ease energy bills, and gas standing charges will be removed for around 23 million homes. The surcharge on bank profits rises by 3 percentage points to 6% on a temporary basis, from January for 15 months, and gambling firms and vape shops face new taxes.
The National Living Wage rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, the 5p fuel duty cut is extended to 30 June 2027, tariffs come off more than 100 grocery products and a First-Time Buyer ISA replaces the Lifetime ISA.
The Office for Budget Responsibility put headroom against the fiscal rule at £15bn in 2029/30, rising to £22bn the following year. It raised growth forecasts to 1.2% this year and 1% next, and said debt interest will cost £14bn more this year. Healey promised no tax rises on wages or dividends.
levels.why: It sets what people pay in tax, how much help they get with bills and how the government borrows.

levels.headline: Chancellor Healey's first Budget: energy help, bank tax and a pay rise for low earners
levels.body:
John Healey set out his first Budget as Chancellor on 28 October 2026. Twenty million households will get a £100 payment toward winter energy bills, and gas standing charges are scrapped for around 23 million homes. Banks will pay a higher temporary surcharge of 6% on profits, starting in January and lasting 15 months. New taxes hit gambling companies and vape shops.
The National Living Wage goes up 3.9% to £13.21 an hour. The 5p cut in fuel duty is extended until 30 June 2027, tariffs on more than 100 groceries are removed, and a First-Time Buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA.
The independent OBR says the government has £15bn of room against its fiscal rule in 2029/30, rising to £22bn in 2030/31. It expects debt interest to cost £14bn more this year. Healey pledged no tax rises on wages or dividends.
levels.why: Budget choices decide who pays more and who gets help during a cost of living squeeze.

levels.headline: The Budget: bills help, a tax on bank profits and a higher minimum wage
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October 2026. The government will pay £100 to 20 million households to help with energy bills over the colder months, and will end gas standing charges for about 23 million homes. Banks will pay more tax, with their profits surcharge rising to 6% for 15 months from January. Gambling firms and vape shops face new taxes too.
The National Living Wage will rise 3.9% to £13.21 an hour. Fuel duty will stay lower until 30 June 2027, and import taxes on more than 100 grocery items will be removed. A new ISA for first-time buyers replaces the Lifetime ISA.
The official forecaster, the OBR, says the government has £15bn of spare room against its borrowing rules by 2029/30. Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends.
levels.why: It shows how the government is trying to ease living costs while keeping the public finances in order.

levels.headline: Chancellor John Healey sets out his first Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey presented his first Budget on 28 October 2026. The government will give £100 to 20 million households to help with winter energy bills, and remove gas standing charges, the fixed daily fee on bills, for around 23 million homes.
To raise money, banks will pay a higher surcharge on their profits of 6% for 15 months from January, and gambling firms and vape shops face new taxes. The National Living Wage, the minimum pay for adults, goes up 3.9% to £13.21 an hour. The cut in fuel duty continues until 30 June 2027, and taxes on over 100 grocery imports are scrapped. A new ISA for first-time buyers replaces the Lifetime ISA.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility said the government has £15bn of room in its borrowing rules by 2029/30. Healey said wages and dividends would not face higher taxes.
levels.why: The Budget affects wages, bills and prices for millions of households.

levels.headline: The Budget: help with energy bills, a bank tax and a pay rise for low earners
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey, the minister in charge of the country's money, gave his first Budget on 28 October 2026. A Budget is the yearly plan for tax and spending. He said 20 million households will get £100 to help with winter energy bills. Gas standing charges, the fixed daily fee on a bill, will be removed for about 23 million homes.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits for 15 months from January, and gambling firms and vape shops will face new taxes. The minimum pay for adults rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, and the lower tax on fuel lasts until 30 June 2027.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility says the government has some room in its borrowing rules. Healey said wages and dividends will not face higher taxes.
levels.why: It affects bills, pay and prices for millions of families.

levels.headline: The Budget: £100 for energy bills, a bank tax and a bigger minimum wage
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the minister in charge of the country's money. John Healey is the new Chancellor, and on 28 October 2026 he announced his first Budget, a yearly plan for taxes and spending.
He said 20 million homes will get £100 to help pay for heating in the colder months. He also said gas standing charges, a fixed daily fee on bills, will be removed for around 23 million homes. Banks will pay a higher tax on their profits for 15 months from January. Gambling firms and vape shops will pay new taxes.
The minimum wage for adults goes up 3.9% to £13.21 an hour. Petrol and diesel will stay a bit cheaper because a tax cut continues until 30 June 2027. Taxes on over 100 foods brought in from abroad will go. An independent group of experts says the government has some spare room in its plans. Healey promised no tax rises on wages.
levels.why: It decides how much help families get and who pays for it.

levels.headline: A new Chancellor's plan: help with bills and a tax on banks
levels.body:
Each year the government says how it will raise money and spend it. This plan is called the Budget. On 28 October 2026, the new Chancellor, John Healey, gave his first one. The Chancellor is the minister who looks after the country's money.
He said 20 million homes will get £100 to help with winter heating bills. Gas standing charges, a fixed daily fee that you pay even if you use no gas, will go for about 23 million homes. Banks will pay more tax on their profits for 15 months. Gambling firms and vape shops will also pay new taxes.
People on the lowest pay will get a rise. The minimum wage for adults goes up to £13.21 an hour. Fuel will be a bit cheaper for longer. Healey said he will not raise taxes on wages.
levels.why: It affects the bills families pay and the pay people take home.

levels.headline: The new Chancellor says how he will spend and tax
levels.body:
Every year, the government decides how to collect money from people and companies and how to spend it. This yearly plan is called the Budget. The person in charge is the Chancellor. His name is John Healey, and this was his first Budget, on 28 October 2026.
He said that 20 million homes will get £100 to help pay for heating this winter. He said banks will pay extra tax on their profits for a while. Companies that run gambling and shops that sell vapes will also pay new taxes.
The lowest pay allowed for adults is called the minimum wage. It will go up to £13.21 an hour. He also said petrol and diesel will stay a little cheaper for longer, and some foods will cost less to bring into the country.
levels.why: It helps decide how much money families have and what the country can afford.

levels.headline: A plan for the country's money
levels.body:
Imagine your school has a pot of money. Someone must decide what to spend it on and how to collect it. In the UK, that job belongs to the Chancellor. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he shared a big plan for the country's money. It is called the Budget.
He said families will get some money to help pay for heating when it is cold. Banks, which look after people's money, will have to pay a bit more tax for a while. Grown-ups who work for the lowest pay will get a rise, to £13.21 for every hour they work.
He said some food from other countries will cost less. Petrol will stay a bit cheaper for longer too. He promised not to take more tax from people's pay.
levels.why: It decides how much help families get with bills.

levels.headline: Money for heating
levels.body:
Winter is cold, and homes need heating. Heating costs money. The person who looks after the country's money is called the Chancellor. His name is John Healey. He has made a plan to help.
He said that lots of families will get £100 to help pay for heating. It is like when a grown-up gives you a little extra pocket money for something you need.
He also said banks will pay a bit more to the government for a while. And grown-ups who work for the smallest pay will get a rise for each hour they work. Some food will cost less too. He wants families to have a bit more money left at the end of the month.
levels.why: It helps families stay warm and pay their bills.

headline: Burnham says an EU rejoin referendum is 'possible' in a future manifesto ahead of 20 November summit

terms.meaning: A document where a party sets out what it promises to do if it wins an election.
The European area where people cross borders without passport checks.

levels.headline: Burnham says an EU rejoin referendum is 'possible' in a future manifesto ahead of 20 November summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the EU could feature in a future election manifesto, while insisting that holding one now would not be the right thing to do. He made the comments to the BBC this week. A general election is not expected before 2029.
A UK-EU summit is due on 20 November, where Burnham has said he will set out the options for Britain's long-term relationship with its European partners. Open issues include youth mobility and tuition fees for EU students. He has called for an "honest discussion" on free movement, while ruling out ever joining the Schengen zone or adopting the euro.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has argued the UK should first join the EU's defence frameworks before any talk of membership, and that ties should develop gradually. It is unclear whether a deal can be reached by the summit.
levels.why: Britain's future relationship with its biggest trading partner affects trade, prices, travel and study.

levels.headline: Burnham leaves door open to a future vote on rejoining the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC it is "possible" a future election manifesto could include a referendum on rejoining the EU, though he called a vote "the wrong thing to do right now". No general election is expected before 2029.
The next key date is a UK-EU summit on 20 November. Burnham says he will lay out the different options for the long-term relationship to the country. Youth mobility and tuition fees for EU students are among the unresolved issues. He wants an "honest discussion" on free movement but has ruled out joining Schengen, the passport-free travel area, or adopting the euro.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says the UK should first join the bloc's defence frameworks and build ties step by step. It is not clear whether the two sides can agree a deal before the summit.
levels.why: The government's stance shapes the UK's economic and political direction for years.

levels.headline: Burnham says a vote on rejoining the EU is possible, but not now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is possible that a future election manifesto could promise a referendum on rejoining the EU. He told the BBC that holding such a vote now would not be right. A general election is not due until 2029.
A summit between the UK and the EU takes place on 20 November. Burnham says he will explain the options for Britain's long-term relationship with Europe. Questions still to be settled include whether young people can live and work more easily across borders, and fees for EU students at UK universities. He wants an honest discussion about free movement but rules out joining the Schengen travel area or the euro.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, thinks the UK should first join EU defence schemes and move gradually.
levels.why: It shows how the UK may reshape its relationship with Europe after Brexit.

levels.headline: Burnham does not rule out an EU rejoin referendum in a future manifesto
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is possible that a referendum on rejoining the EU could appear in a party's manifesto at a future election. A manifesto is the list of promises a party makes before voters go to the polls. He said a vote now would not be right. The next election is not expected before 2029.
On 20 November the UK and EU meet for a summit. Burnham says he will set out the choices for Britain's long-term relationship with its neighbours. Issues still open include youth mobility and university fees for EU students. He wants an honest discussion about free movement but will not join Schengen, the area with no passport checks, or adopt the euro.
Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, says the UK should first join EU defence plans and build trust slowly.
levels.why: Decisions here affect trade, jobs and how easily people can travel and study abroad.

levels.headline: Burnham says a future vote on rejoining the EU is possible, but not now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is possible that a referendum on rejoining the European Union could appear in a party's manifesto, which is its list of election promises. He said holding a vote now would not be right. A general election is not expected before 2029.
On 20 November, the UK and EU will hold a summit. Burnham says he will set out the choices for Britain's long-term relationship with Europe. Open questions include youth mobility, which would let young people live and work more easily abroad, and fees for EU students.
He wants an honest talk about free movement but has ruled out joining Schengen, the passport-free travel area, or the euro. The EU's Kaja Kallas says the UK should start with defence.
levels.why: It could change trade, travel and study across Europe.

levels.headline: Burnham says a vote on rejoining the EU could happen one day
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union in 2020, a change known as Brexit. Now Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that a referendum on rejoining could be part of a party's promises at a future election. Those promises are written in a manifesto. He said a vote now would not be the right thing. The next election is not expected before 2029.
On 20 November, the UK and EU leaders will meet. Burnham says he will explain the choices for Britain's future ties with Europe. Things still to be agreed include how easily young people can live and work abroad, and the fees EU students pay at UK universities.
He does not want to join the passport-free travel area called Schengen, or to use the euro. An EU leader said the UK should start with defence and go slowly.
levels.why: It could change trade, travel and study for people across the UK.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says rejoining the EU is possible someday, but not now
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union a few years ago. This was called Brexit. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the UK might vote on joining again one day. He said a party could put that idea in its manifesto, which is a list of promises before an election. But he said a vote now would not be right.
The next election is not due until 2029. Before then, on 20 November, UK and EU leaders will meet. Burnham plans to explain the choices for how close Britain should be to Europe. Some open questions are how easily young people can work abroad and what EU students pay at UK universities.
He does not want to use the euro or join the area where people cross borders without passports.
levels.why: It affects how easily we trade, travel and study in Europe.

levels.headline: Could the UK rejoin the EU one day?
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a club of European countries called the European Union. It left in 2020. That was called Brexit. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the UK might vote on joining the club again in the future. Not now, though. He says now is the wrong time.
A party writes down its promises before an election. That list is called a manifesto. Burnham said a vote on rejoining could be on that list one day. The next election is not due until 2029.
On 20 November, UK and EU leaders will meet to talk. Burnham wants to explain the different choices for the future. They will talk about things like whether young people can study and work in other countries more easily.
levels.why: It could change how easy it is to travel, work or study in Europe.

levels.headline: The UK and its European neighbours
levels.body:
A group of countries in Europe works together as the European Union. The UK used to belong, but left in 2020. Some people want the UK to join again. Others do not. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the UK might hold a vote on this one day. But he says now is not the right time.
On 20 November, leaders of the UK and the EU will meet. They will talk about how closely they should work together. One idea is to make it easier for young people to work or study in each other's countries.
Before an election, each party writes down what it promises. That list is called a manifesto. The next election is not until 2029. So the idea could appear in a manifesto a few years from now.
levels.why: It shapes how close the UK stays to its nearest neighbours.

levels.headline: Friends across the sea
levels.body:
Imagine your school is in a club with other schools nearby. The schools share sports days and trips. Then your school leaves the club. Now some people wonder if it should join again.
That is a bit like the UK and the European Union. The UK was in the club of European countries and left in 2020. The leader of the UK is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham. He says the UK might have a vote one day on whether to join again. But he says not now.
On 20 November, leaders from the UK and the club will meet and talk about how to work together. They may talk about making it easier for young people to study and work in each other's countries.
levels.why: It could change how easy it is to visit and learn in other countries.

headline: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action ban as police arrest supporters

terms.meaning: Banning an organisation under terrorism law, making membership or support a crime.
A court process that checks whether a public body acted lawfully.

levels.headline: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action ban as police arrest supporters
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court heard an appeal on 4 and 5 November 2026 against the government's ban on Palestine Action, brought by co-founder Huda Ammori. No ruling has been reported yet. Police arrested supporters outside the court on 4 November. They said 25 people were detained on suspicion of supporting a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act, with more arrests expected.
Permission to appeal was granted in part on 29 July, limited to the argument that the Home Secretary did not follow her own published policy on proscription. The High Court had ruled in Ammori's favour in February, finding the ban disproportionate, but the Court of Appeal reversed that in June and found for the Home Office.
Ammori has said that if she loses she will take the case to the European Court of Human Rights.
levels.why: The case tests how far the state can go in banning groups under terrorism law.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears challenge to Palestine Action proscription
levels.body:
The Supreme Court heard Huda Ammori's challenge to the ban on Palestine Action on 4 and 5 November 2026. A judgment has not yet been reported. On 4 November police arrested supporters outside the court; they said 25 people were held on suspicion of supporting a banned group under the Terrorism Act and that further arrests were expected.
The court agreed to hear only a narrow argument: that the Home Secretary failed to follow her own published policy when banning the group. The High Court sided with Ammori in February, calling the ban disproportionate. In June the Court of Appeal overturned that and backed the Home Office.
Ammori has said she will go to the European Court of Human Rights if she loses in the UK.
levels.why: It could set limits on the government's power to ban protest groups.

levels.headline: Palestine Action ban goes before the Supreme Court
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court has held a two-day hearing on the ban on the group Palestine Action. The appeal was brought by co-founder Huda Ammori and took place on 4 and 5 November. No decision has been reported. Outside the court on 4 November, police arrested supporters; they said 25 people were held on suspicion of backing a banned group under the Terrorism Act, and more arrests might follow.
The Supreme Court allowed only one argument to go ahead: that the Home Secretary did not follow her own published policy on bans. In February the High Court ruled for Ammori, saying the ban was out of proportion, but the Court of Appeal reversed this in June.
Ammori says she will take the case to the European Court of Human Rights if she loses.
levels.why: The ruling will shape how terrorism law can be used against protest groups.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears appeal over the ban on Palestine Action
levels.body:
The Supreme Court, the highest court in the UK, has heard an appeal against the government's ban on Palestine Action. The hearing took place on 4 and 5 November. Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the group, brought the case. No ruling has been announced yet. Police arrested supporters outside the building on 4 November. They said 25 people were detained on suspicion of supporting a banned group under the Terrorism Act, and more arrests were expected.
The court will look only at whether the Home Secretary followed her own published policy when she banned the group. The High Court found the ban disproportionate in February, but the Court of Appeal disagreed in June.
Ammori has said she will go to the European Court of Human Rights if she loses.
levels.why: It raises questions about protest, free speech and the power to ban groups.

levels.headline: UK's top court hears case about banning Palestine Action
levels.body:
The highest court in the UK, the Supreme Court, has heard a case about a ban on a group called Palestine Action. Under terrorism law, the government can ban a group, which makes it a crime to belong to it or support it. The ban was challenged by one of its founders, Huda Ammori. The hearing was on 4 and 5 November, and there is no decision yet.
Outside the court on 4 November, police arrested 25 people who they said had shown support for the banned group. More arrests were expected.
The judges will look at one question only. Did the Home Secretary follow the government's own written rules when she banned the group? A lower court said the ban went too far in February, but another court disagreed in June. Ammori says she will go to a European court if she loses.
levels.why: Courts decide how much power the government has to ban groups.

levels.headline: Top court hears case on banning a protest group
levels.body:
The UK's top court, the Supreme Court, has been looking at a case about a group called Palestine Action. The government banned this group using terrorism laws. That means it is a crime to join it or show support for it. One of the group's founders, Huda Ammori, is challenging the ban.
The court met on 4 and 5 November. It has not given its decision yet. Outside, police arrested 25 people who were showing support for the group. The police said they expected more arrests.
The judges are only looking at one question. Did the Home Secretary follow the government's own written rules when she made the ban? In February one court said the ban went too far. In June a higher court said it was fine. Ammori says she will go to a European court if she loses.
levels.why: It is about where the line sits between protest and breaking the law.

levels.headline: A court looks at the ban on a protest group
levels.body:
A group called Palestine Action was banned by the government. The ban means it is against the law to join the group or to say you support it. The group's co-founder, Huda Ammori, does not agree with the ban. She asked the top court in the UK, the Supreme Court, to look at it. The judges heard the case on 4 and 5 November. They have not decided yet.
Outside the court, police arrested 25 people who showed support for the group. Police said more arrests might come.
The judges will only check one thing: did the government follow its own rules when it made the ban? Ammori says that if she loses she will ask a court in Europe to look at it.
levels.why: It tests how the government may use its power to ban groups.

levels.headline: The top court looks at a banned group
levels.body:
In the UK, the government can ban a group if it thinks the group is dangerous. After that, it is against the law to join the group. A group called Palestine Action was banned. One of its founders does not think that was fair. So she asked the highest court in the country to look at it.
The judges met on 4 and 5 November. They listen to both sides and then decide. They have not told everyone their decision yet. Outside the court, some people came to show support. The police arrested 25 of them.
The judges will check if the government followed its own rules when it banned the group. If the founder loses, she says she will ask a court in Europe to look.
levels.why: Courts make sure the government follows its own rules.

levels.headline: A court checks the rules
levels.body:
A grown-up in the government can say that a group is not allowed. Then people must not join it. A group called Palestine Action was told it was not allowed. One of the people who started it, Huda Ammori, thinks that was not fair. So she asked the biggest court in the country to check.
The judges listened to both sides on 4 and 5 November. They have not said who is right yet. Some people stood outside to show support. The police arrested 25 of them.
The judges are checking if the government followed its own rules. It is a bit like a referee checking whether a goal was fair.
levels.why: It makes sure everyone, even the government, follows the rules.

levels.headline: The referee checks the rules
levels.body:
In football, a referee makes sure everyone follows the rules. In a country, judges do a similar job. They check that the government follows the rules too.
A group of people called Palestine Action was told by the government that it was not allowed to exist. One of its founders, Huda Ammori, did not agree. She asked the biggest court in the country to look at it.
The judges met for two days, on 4 and 5 November. They listened carefully to both sides. They have not decided yet. Some people stood outside the court to show support. The police arrested 25 of them.
The judges will decide if the government played by its own rules.
levels.why: Judges help keep things fair, even for grown-ups in charge.

headline: Democrats win control of both houses of Congress in midterms, a rebuke to Trump

terms.meaning: US elections held halfway through a president's term, choosing members of Congress.
A president's power to block a law passed by Congress.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of both houses of Congress in midterms, a rebuke to Trump
levels.body:
Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections held on 3 November 2026, according to several outlets. Counts were still shifting, and reports differ on the exact House total, so it is best to treat the final seat numbers as unsettled.
Control of Congress lets Democrats launch investigations with subpoena power. Analysts note they will lack the numbers to override a presidential veto, and Senate filibuster rules still apply. President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the result and told CNBC he can work with Democrats on many things, but said elsewhere that he plans to use his veto.
Coverage points to voter anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump's war with Iran, as well as corruption concerns and the politics of data centres. Markets reacted sharply, with technology shares selling off on fears for the AI buildout.
levels.why: It changes what the US president can pass, and affects foreign policy and global markets.

Trump said he would accept the result and could work with Democrats on many things, but also said he plans to use his veto.
Analysts say voters were angry about the cost of living, tariffs and the war with Iran, and also worried about corruption and data-centre politics. Technology shares fell sharply afterwards as investors feared a slowdown in AI spending.
levels.why: The result will shape US policy at home and abroad for the next two years.

levels.headline: The Democrats win a big election in America
levels.body:

The Democratic Party won control of Congress, which is the group that makes American laws. It has two parts, the House and the Senate. Counting was still going on, and news reports gave different numbers.

levels.headline: An election in America changes who is in charge of making laws
levels.body:
In America, the president and the people who make the laws can belong to different groups, called parties. On 3 November there was an election. The Democratic Party won control of Congress, the group that makes laws. The president, Donald Trump, is from the other party, the Republicans.
This means the Democrats can ask questions and look into what the president is doing. If Congress makes a law, the president can say no. That is called a veto. The Democrats do not have enough votes to get around a veto.
People voted this way because they were upset. They said things cost too much and they did not like the war with Iran. Trump says he accepts the result.
levels.why: It shows that voters can change who holds power.

levels.headline: Voters in America choose a new team to make laws

The country's president, Donald Trump, is from a different team called the Republicans. The two teams will now have to work together, or argue. The Democrats can ask lots of questions about what the president is doing. The president can say no to a law. That is called a veto.
Many voters were unhappy because food and other things cost a lot. Some did not like the war with Iran. Trump said he accepts the result.
levels.why: It shows how voters can change who is in charge.

levels.headline: America picks a new team
levels.body:
Imagine your class votes for a new class captain, and the teacher likes someone else. The captain and the teacher would have to find a way to work together.
Something like this happened in America. On 3 November, grown-ups voted. They chose the Democratic team to lead the group that makes the laws. The country's leader, President Trump, is from another team. He can say no to new laws, and the other team cannot always stop him.
Many voters were upset because things cost too much. Others did not like a war far away. President Trump said he would accept the result. Now the two sides must find a way to work together.
levels.why: It shows that people's votes can change who is in charge.

levels.headline: US says it carried out 'minor strikes' on Iran as missiles reportedly hit Qeshm Island, while Trump claims progress in Qatar-led talks
levels.body:
President Donald Trump said on Friday 6 November that the United States carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, saying they knocked out an anti-aircraft device in about 15 minutes, "maybe five". He did not explicitly say where. Iranian state media reported that two missiles hit the Suza area of Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, and the Tasnim agency said there was no official information on damage.
The United States had already struck the island on Monday 3 November, which a US official called a "defensive measure" after Iranians used surface-to-air missiles against American assets. Trump insisted "we are not fighting" and said there had been "a lot of progress" in negotiations led by Qatar. Iran has said it wants more than "paper commitments" before entering a new phase of diplomatic talks.
The strikes came after the US midterm elections, and analysts had debated whether the vote would push Trump towards escalation or renewed diplomacy. Euronews describes limited new airstrikes in southern Iran, while CNBC notes Trump did not confirm that his strikes were the ones reported on Qeshm.
levels.why: The strikes show that fighting and diplomacy are happening at the same time, which affects oil prices and energy bills worldwide.

levels.headline: Oil prices tumble for the week as investors weigh Iran conflict risk after the midterms
levels.body:
Oil prices fell sharply over the week to 6 November 2026. Brent crude futures settled at $98.32 a barrel on Friday, up 3 cents on the day, while US West Texas Intermediate settled at $90.83. Brent lost more than 16% over the week and US crude fell nearly 13%.
The decline followed the US midterm elections, which investors saw as improving the chances of a quicker end to the conflict in the Middle East, although uncertainty remains. Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally sees an 80% probability that military fighting resumes and thinks both benchmarks could climb above $100 a barrel.
Trading Economics reported crude oil up about 51% on a year earlier. Its models, which are forecasts and not market prices, put crude at around $107 and Brent near $117 by the end of the quarter. US gasoline was $2.75 a gallon on 6 November.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, heating and the price of almost everything else.

levels.why: It signals whether energy bills and fuel prices may ease or climb again.

levels.headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US to hold talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November
levels.body:
Ukraine, Russia and the United States are due to hold talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November 2026, the first meeting of all three sides since February. Envoy Steve Witkoff said the US will mediate working-level negotiations on security arrangements and de-escalation, and the Kremlin said Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky will lead Russia's team.
Hopes of a breakthrough are low. Russia struck Ukraine heavily after a rare truce ended at the weekend, including 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles in one overnight attack, according to President Zelenskyy. Ukraine says Russia refused an offer to extend the truce. Kyiv wants guarantees against future aggression, while Moscow wants limits on NATO's presence in Eastern Europe.
European leaders are pushing for a seat at the table, and Poland has warned allies not to negotiate with Russia over Eastern Europe's head. Officials hope for progress on prisoner exchanges and protecting energy infrastructure.
levels.why: The talks could shape Europe's security and the future of the war.

Ukraine says Russia refused to extend the truce. Ukraine wants security guarantees, while Russia wants limits on NATO forces in Eastern Europe.
France, Germany, the UK, the European Commission and NATO are ready to join wider talks afterwards, and Poland warns against deals made over Eastern Europe's head. European officials hope for agreement on prisoner swaps and protecting energy sites.
levels.why: Europe's safety and its energy supplies depend on how this war ends.

levels.headline: Paraguay protests erupt after Ueno Bank collapse as President Peña faces impeachment
levels.body:
Thousands of Paraguayans took to the streets this week after the central bank took control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall. The bank had close to three million customers, who were suddenly unable to reach their accounts. Eight senior executives, including chief executive Miguel Vázquez, were arrested on Wednesday.
President Santiago Peña offered to resign, but reports differ on whether he has left office. The indictment cites conflict of interest and alleged embezzlement of pension funds. Peña held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank until last year and defended the bank and its regulator as recently as last month.
